en.question: Is plastic dangerous for dogs?
en.answer: Plastic is non-toxic but can cause life-threatening intestinal obstruction. The danger depends on the size and shape of the plastic object relative to your dog. Items larger than 2cm wide are unlikely to pass through the pylorus (stomach exit) or ileocecal junction. Sharp plastic edges can also cause GI perforation.

en.question: Symptoms of plastic blockage in dogs?
en.answer: Symptoms appear within 2-48 hours: repeated vomiting (especially after eating), loss of appetite, lethargy, abdominal pain, absence of bowel movements, and dehydration. A complete obstruction causes persistent vomiting, dehydration, and shock within 24-72 hours. This is a surgical emergency.

en.question: How long does it take for plastic to pass through a dog?
en.answer: Small plastic pieces (under 2cm) typically pass through the GI tract within 24-48 hours and appear in stool. Larger items may take 3-5 days or become lodged. If plastic has not passed within 48 hours, or if vomiting occurs, veterinary intervention is required.

en.question: When should I call the vet if my dog ate plastic?
en.answer: Call your vet immediately if: (1) the plastic object is larger than 2cm in any dimension, (2) your dog vomits more than once, (3) no bowel movement occurs within 48 hours, (4) your dog shows abdominal pain or lethargy, or (5) the plastic piece is sharp/rigid. Do NOT wait for symptoms if the object is large.

en.question: Which human medications are most toxic to dogs?
en.answer: The most dangerous human medications for dogs include: (1) NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) — GI ulcers and kidney failure at 50mg/kg. (5) Benzodiazepines — paradoxical agitation. (6) Vitamin D supplements — fatal hypercalcemia.

en.question: What are the symptoms of ibuprofen poisoning in dogs?
en.answer: Symptoms appear within 1-4 hours: vomiting (possibly with blood), loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Megaesophagus (enlarged esophagus) can occur with chronic exposure. Treatment includes activated charcoal, gastroprotectants, IV fluids, and blood monitoring.

en.question: Is rat poison deadly to dogs?
en.answer: Yes, rat poison (rodenticide) is one of the most deadly toxins for dogs. There are two main types: (1) Anticoagulant rodenticides (warfarin, bromadiolone, brodifacoum) — prevent blood clotting, causing fatal internal bleeding. Single-dose types require one feeding; multiple-dose types are cumulative. (2) Neurotoxic rodenticides (bromethalin, strychnine, cholecalciferol) — cause brain swelling, seizures, or hypercalcium within hours. Without treatment, mortality rates are 50-90%.

en.question: What are the symptoms of rat poison in dogs?
en.answer: Anticoagulant symptoms appear 2-5 days after ingestion: weakness, pale gums, coughing blood, bloody vomit/diarrhea, nosebleeds, and collapse. Neurotoxic (bromethalin) symptoms appear within 2-24 hours: severe muscle tremors, seizures, ataxia, and paralysis. Cholecalciferol causes kidney failure with increased thirst/urination within 12-36 hours.

en.question: Can my dog survive rat poison?
en.answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. Anticoagulant poisoning is treatable with Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks; survival rate is 80-90% if treated before symptoms appear. Bromethalin has no antidote — treatment is supportive care (activated charcoal, mannitol for brain swelling) with 50-70% survival if treated early. Strychnine and cholecalciferol also require immediate veterinary intervention.

en.question: What should I do if my dog ate rat poison?
en.answer: Treat this as a dire emergency: (1) Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. (2) Go to the nearest emergency vet NOW — do not wait for symptoms. (3) Bring the product label to identify the active ingredient. (4) Induced vomiting within 1-2 hours may help prevent absorption. (5) Even if your dog seems fine, delayed symptoms are common and early treatment is life-saving.

hi.answer: Yes, rat poison (rodenticide) is one of the most deadly toxins for dogs. There are two main types: (1) Anticoagulant rodenticides (warfarin, bromadiolone, brodifacoum) — prevent blood clotting, causing fatal internal bleeding. Single-dose types require one feeding; multiple-dose types are cumulative. (2) Neurotoxic rodenticides (bromethalin, strychnine, cholecalciferol) — cause brain swelling, seizures, or hypercalcium within hours. Without treatment, mortality rates are 50-90%.

hi.question: What are the symptoms of rat poison in dogs?
hi.answer: Anticoagulant symptoms appear 2-5 days after ingestion: weakness, pale gums, coughing blood, bloody vomit/diarrhea, nosebleeds, and collapse. Neurotoxic (bromethalin) symptoms appear within 2-24 hours: severe muscle tremors, seizures, ataxia, and paralysis. Cholecalciferol causes kidney failure with increased thirst/urination within 12-36 hours.

hi.question: Can my dog survive rat poison?
hi.answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. Anticoagulant poisoning is treatable with Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks; survival rate is 80-90% if treated before symptoms appear. Bromethalin has no antidote — treatment is supportive care (activated charcoal, mannitol for brain swelling) with 50-70% survival if treated early. Strychnine and cholecalciferol also require immediate veterinary intervention.

hi.question: What should I do if my dog ate rat poison?

(3) Bring the product label to identify the active ingredient. (4) Induced vomiting within 1-2 hours may help prevent absorption. (5) Even if your dog seems fine, delayed symptoms are common and early treatment is life-saving.

en.question: Is marijuana toxic to dogs?
en.answer: Yes, THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) is toxic to dogs. Dogs have more cannabinoid receptors (CB1) in the brain than humans, making them significantly more sensitive. Edibles (gummies, brownies, cookies) are especially dangerous due to high THC concentration — one gummy can contain 10-100mg THC, which is toxic to most dogs.

en.question: What are the symptoms of marijuana poisoning in dogs?
en.answer: Symptoms appear within 30-90 minutes: dazed appearance, stumbling/ataxia, urinary incontinence (dripping urine), drooling, dilated pupils, vomiting, tremors, bradycardia (slow heart rate), hypothermia, and in severe cases: seizures or coma. Be honest with your vet — marijuana toxicosis is rarely fatal, and honesty ensures proper treatment.

en.question: Are marijuana edibles more dangerous than dried cannabis?
en.answer: Yes, edibles are significantly more dangerous: (1) High THC concentration (10-100mg per piece), (2) Often contain chocolate (double toxicity), (3) Faster absorption from GI tract, (4) Dogs eat multiple pieces quickly. Edibles account for the majority of severe cannabis toxicosis cases in dogs.

en.question: Can a dog die from eating marijuana?
en.answer: Fatalities from marijuana alone are rare in dogs — the LD50 is very high (over 3g/kg of THC). However, edibles pose additional risks: chocolate toxicity, xylitol in some CBD products, and overdose from multiple ingestion. Death is more likely from complications (aspiration pneumonia, hypothermia) or combined toxins. Always seek veterinary care.

en.question: Should I tell my vet my dog ate marijuana?
en.answer: Yes, always be honest. Veterinarians are required to treat, not report, pet poisonings. Knowing your dog ate marijuana ensures they provide appropriate care: inducing vomiting (if early), activated charcoal, IV fluids, thermoregulation, and monitoring heart rate. Without this information, your dog may undergo unnecessary tests or receive inappropriate treatment.

en.answer: Xylitol is toxic to dogs at doses as low as 0.1g/kg for hypoglycemia and 0.5g/kg for liver failure. en.question: What are the symptoms of xylitol poisoning in dogs?
en.answer: Symptoms appear within 10-60 minutes (sometimes delayed 12 hours): vomiting, lethargy, weakness, collapse, tremors, seizures, and coma — these result from hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Liver failure symptoms (jaundice, coagulopathy) may be delayed 12-72 hours. Even small amounts cause dangerously low blood sugar.

en.question: Why is xylitol toxic to dogs but not humans?
en.answer: In dogs, xylitol is rapidly absorbed and triggers a massive insulin release from the pancreas — 6-7x more than glucose would. This causes profound hypoglycemia. Humans do not have this insulin response. Additionally, xylitol causes dose-dependent hepatocellular necrosis in dogs through mechanisms not seen in humans.

en.question: What products contain xylitol?
en.answer: Xylitol is found in: sugar-free gum, mints, peanut butter (some brands), toothpaste, mouthwash, nasal sprays, chewable vitamins, baked goods, ice cream, and "birch sugar" sold as a sweetener. Some brands: Trident, Orbit, Ice Breakers, Eclipse. Always check ingredient lists before giving human food to dogs.

en.question: Can a dog survive xylitol poisoning?
en.answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. If caught within 30 minutes, induced vomiting prevents absorption. If hypoglycemia has begun, IV dextrose corrects blood sugar. en.answer: As little as 1 teaspoon (5ml) of antifreeze can kill a 10lb (4.5kg) dog. The lethal dose of ethylene glycol is approximately 4.4ml per kg of body weight. This makes antifreeze one of the most dangerous household toxins for pets.

en.question: How fast does antifreeze kill dogs?

en.question: Is chocolate toxic to cats?
en.answer: Yes, chocolate is toxic to cats — often more so than to dogs relative to body weight. Cats are more sensitive to theobromine because they metabolize it more slowly. The same toxic principle applies: theobromine and caffeine cause CNS stimulation, cardiac arrhythmias, and potentially seizures.

en.question: Why are cats more sensitive than dogs?
en.answer: Cats have lower activity of cytochrome P450 enzymes responsible for metabolizing theobromine. While dogs take 17+ hours to clear theobromine, cats may take even longer. Additionally, cats typically weigh less (4-6kg average), so the dose-per-kg ratio from the same amount of chocolate is higher.

en.question: How much chocolate is toxic to cats?
en.answer: Milk chocolate becomes toxic at approximately 0.5 oz per pound of body weight. Dark chocolate and baking chocolate are 2-5x more toxic. For a 5kg (11lb) cat, as little as 20g of milk chocolate (about half a standard bar) can cause symptoms. Baking chocolate is lethal at 5-10g for an average cat.

en.question: What should I do if my cat ate chocolate?
en.answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your vet immediately. Cats are more sensitive than dogs — even small amounts are concerning. Bring the chocolate packaging to identify theobromine content. Do NOT wait for symptoms, as cardiac arrhythmias can be sudden and fatal.

en.question: Are onions toxic to cats?
en.answer: Yes, onions are highly toxic to cats — more so than dogs relative to body weight. Onions contain N-propyl disulfide and thiosulfates that cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, leading to Heinz body hemolytic anemia. Cats are uniquely vulnerable because their hemoglobin is more susceptible to oxidation, and they produce methemoglobin more readily.

en.question: How much onion is toxic to cats?
en.answer: Even small amounts are dangerous. Toxic effects can occur at 5g/kg body weight (about 1 tablespoon for a 4kg cat). Regular consumption of smaller amounts (even trace amounts in baby food or broth) can cause cumulative damage. Raw, cooked, powdered, and dehydrated onions are all toxic.

en.question: What are the symptoms of onion poisoning in cats?
en.answer: Symptoms appear 1-5 days after ingestion: pale or yellow gums (anemia/jaundice), weakness, rapid breathing, reddish-brown urine (hemoglobinuria), vomiting, and lethargy. Heinz body anemia is confirmed by blood smear showing damaged red blood cells. Severe cases require blood transfusion.

en.question: Can onion powder hurt cats?
en.answer: Yes, onion powder is concentrated and especially dangerous. Even small amounts in broth, gravy, baby food, or treats can cause toxicity. Many commercial products contain hidden onion or garlic powder. Always check ingredient labels before sharing human food with cats.

en.question: Why are essential oils toxic to cats?
en.answer: Cats lack UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) enzymes needed to metabolize certain compounds in essential oils (terpenes, phenols, ketones). This makes them 10x more sensitive than dogs to tea tree oil, citrus oils, eucalyptus, peppermint, and pine oils. Even topical application on skin can cause toxicity if the cat licks it off.

en.question: Which essential oils are most dangerous for cats?
en.answer: Most dangerous: Tea tree (melaleuca), wintergreen, peppermint, pine, eucalyptus, citrus (limonene, linalool), cinnamon, clove, ylang ylang, birch, and thyme. Tea tree oil is most commonly reported — even 10-20mL on skin can be fatal. Diffusers are also dangerous as cats inhale droplets and groom them from fur.

en.question: What are the symptoms of essential oil poisoning in cats?
en.answer: Symptoms depend on oil type and route: (1) Ingestion: drooling, vomiting, tremors, ataxia, weakness, hypothermia. (2) Skin absorption: lethargy, hypersalivation, liver damage. (3) Inhalation: respiratory distress, aspiration pneumonia. Tea tree oil specifically causes severe hypothermia and ataxia within 2-8 hours.

en.question: Are essential oil diffusers dangerous for cats?
en.answer: Yes, diffusers pose three risks: (1) Inhaled droplets settle on fur and are groomed off, causing ingestion. (2) Volatilized oils irritate feline respiratory passages (cats have efficient smell but sensitive airways). (3) Concentrated oil in the diffuser water can be spilled and licked. Use diffusers only in well-ventilated rooms your cat cannot access.

en.question: Why is fishing line so dangerous for cats?
en.answer: Fishing line is a linear foreign body — when swallowed, it anchors at one end (under tongue, in stomach, or at pylorus) while the rest extends through the intestines. Peristalsis pulls the line taut, causing the intestine to accordion-pleat around it. The line then saws through the intestinal wall, causing multiple perforations, peritonitis, and death if not surgically removed.

en.question: What are the symptoms of linear foreign body in cats?
en.answer: Symptoms include: string visible under tongue or protruding from anus, vomiting (especially after eating), drooling, difficulty swallowing, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and fever. CRITICAL: Always check under the tongue and around the base of the tongue — the line may be anchored there.

en.question: Should I pull the string out of my cat?
en.answer: NO! Never pull on a string or line protruding from your cat mouth or anus. The line may be anchored internally — pulling it can saw through the intestinal wall causing perforations. Go to emergency vet immediately for proper removal under anesthesia.

en.question: What is the treatment for fishing line ingestion in cats?
en.answer: Treatment requires emergency surgery (enterotomy or gastrotomy) to remove the line. Multiple incisions may be needed along the intestine to release the plicated segments. IV antibiotics treat peritonitis, and fluids correct dehydration. Prognosis depends on how many perforations occurred — early surgery has 80-90% survival; delayed treatment with multiple perforations has 50-60% survival.

hi.question: How much lily is toxic to cats?
hi.answer: Ingestion of as little as 2-3 petals or leaves, or exposure to pollen (grooming pollen off fur), can cause acute kidney failure. There is no safe amount — any exposure requires emergency veterinary treatment.

hi.question: How long after lily ingestion do symptoms appear?
hi.answer: Vomiting and lethargy begin within 1-6 hours. Kidney damage is detectable within 12-24 hours. Without treatment, kidney failure develops within 24-72 hours and is often fatal. Early IV fluid therapy is critical.

en.title: Step 2: DO NOT Pull Visible String
en.content: If string is hanging from the mouth or anus, do NOT pull it. This can cause the anchored end to cut through intestinal tissue.

en.title: Step 3: Check Under the Tongue
en.content: If safe to do so, check if string is wrapped around the base of the tongue. If so, this is an emergency — go to the vet NOW.

en.title: Step 4: Monitor for Symptoms
en.content: Watch for vomiting, loss of appetite, lethargy, drooling, and inability to defecate. These require emergency surgery.

en.question: Why is string dangerous for cats?
en.answer: String is a "linear foreign body" — it anchors at the base of the tongue or stomach and the rest is pulled through the intestines as they contract. This causes the intestines to "pleat" (bunch up) and the string can cut through the intestinal wall like a wire, causing perforation, peritonitis, and death.

en.question: What are the symptoms of string ingestion?
en.answer: Vomiting, loss of appetite, lethargy, drooling, visible string hanging from the mouth or anus, abdominal pain, and inability to defecate. If you see string, DO NOT pull it — this can cause more damage.

en.question: How is string ingestion treated?
en.answer: Treatment depends on location. If the string is still in the mouth/tongue, your vet may cut it. If it has entered the GI tract, surgery is often required to remove it safely. X-rays and ultrasound help determine the best approach.
